## Proof

**Claim.** The length of the local ring $\mathcal{O}_{Y_x, y}$ is **1**, not $\deg f$.

### Setup and key observation

Let $f: Y \to X$ be finite étale (the topological case is recovered by the same argument, since a finite connected topological cover of Riemann surfaces corresponds to a finite étale morphism of the associated smooth projective curves over $\mathbb{C}$). Let $x = f(y)$ and $Y_x = f^{-1}(x) = Y \times_X \operatorname{Spec} k(x)$ be the scheme-theoretic fibre.

Because $f$ is finite étale, the fibre $Y_x$ is a **finite étale $k(x)$-scheme**. Concretely, if $A = \Gamma(Y_x, \mathcal{O}_{Y_x})$, then $A$ is a finite étale $k(x)$-algebra.

### Structure of finite étale algebras over a field

A standard theorem (see, e.g., SGA 1, or Milne, *Étale Cohomology*) states:

> A finite étale algebra over a field $k$ is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of $k$.

Applying this to $A$ over $k(x)$, we obtain

$$A \;\cong\; \prod_{i=1}^{r} K_i,$$

where each $K_i / k(x)$ is a finite separable field extension, and

$$\sum_{i=1}^{r} [K_i : k(x)] \;=\; \deg f.$$

The points of $Y_x = \operatorname{Spec} A$ are in bijection with the factors $K_i$. Concretely, the point $p_i$ corresponding to $K_i$ has residue field $\kappa(p_i) \cong K_i$.

### The local ring at $y$

The point $y \in Y_x$ corresponds to some factor, say $K_j$. The local ring of $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(\prod_i K_i\bigr)$ at the point $p_j$ is obtained by localizing $A$ at the prime ideal

$$\mathfrak{p}_j = K_1 \times \cdots \times K_{j-1} \times \{0\} \times K_{j+1} \times \cdots \times K_r.$$

Localization at $\mathfrak{p}_j$ kills all factors except the $j$-th:

$$\mathcal{O}_{Y_x, y} \;=\; A_{\mathfrak{p}_j} \;\cong\; K_j.$$

This is a **field** (a finite separable extension of $k(x)$).

### Length computation

The length of a local ring $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ as an $R$-module is the length of a composition series of $R$ as an $R$-module. A local ring has length $1$ if and only if its maximal ideal is zero, i.e., if and only if it is a field.

Since $\mathcal{O}_{Y_x, y} \cong K_j$ is a field, its maximal ideal is $(0)$, and the unique composition series is

$$K_j \supsetneq (0),$$

which has exactly **one** nontrivial step. Therefore

$$\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal{O}_{Y_x,y}} \mathcal{O}_{Y_x, y} \;=\; 1.$$

### Why it is not $\deg f$

The number $\deg f$ does appear, but at the **global** level of the fibre, not the local level:

$$\dim_{k(x)} \Gamma(Y_x, \mathcal{O}_{Y_x}) \;=\; \dim_{k(x)} A \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} [K_i : k(x)] \;=\; \deg f.$$

This is the **degree** of the finite étale $k(x)$-scheme $Y_x$ — equivalently, the length of $A$ as a $k(x)$-module (the total "size" of the fibre). It is the sum of the local contributions over **all** points of the fibre:

$$\deg f \;=\; \sum_{p \in Y_x} [\kappa(p) : k(x)] \;=\; \sum_{p \in Y_x} \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal{O}_{Y_x,p}} \mathcal{O}_{Y_x,p} \cdot [\kappa(p):k(x)] \;=\; \sum_{p \in Y_x} [\kappa(p):k(x)].$$

Each individual summand (the local length at a single point) is $1$, because étaleness forces each local ring to be a field. The degree $\deg f$ is the **sum** of these $1$'s over all $\deg f$ geometric points (counting separable degree), not the local length at any single point.

### Topological case (consistency check)

For a finite degree $d$ connected topological cover of Riemann surfaces, $f$ is a covering map: every fibre has exactly $d$ points, each with a neighbourhood mapping homeomorphically onto a neighbourhood of $x$. The scheme-theoretic fibre is $d$ reduced points, each with local ring $\mathbb{C}$, a field of length $1$. The total $\mathbb{C}$-dimension of $\Gamma(Y_x, -)$ is $d = \deg f$, consistent with the algebraic computation above.

### Conclusion

The length of $\mathcal{O}_{Y_x, y}$ is **1**. The value $\deg f$ is the degree of the entire fibre as a $k(x)$-scheme (the sum of local lengths over all points of the fibre), not the length of the local ring at a single point. Étaleness is precisely the condition that makes every local ring of the fibre a field, forcing each local length to be $1$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
